Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A striped hot air balloon drifting over a lavender field at sunset, with rolling golden hills, a small hilltop village, and a lone oak tree on the right.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

11 stepsFocal point: The striped balloon in the upper left, balanced by the oak tree on the right; the lavender rows lead the eye to the setting sun in the middle. Light: The sun sits low on the horizon just left of center, so the sky glows orange and yellow there, cloud edges facing it are lit gold, and the hillside and lavender tips catch warm light.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 2 inch flat: covering the whole canvas and blending the gradientFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: the round sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1 inch flat: dabbing the cloud massesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat: dry brushing the gold edgesOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #4 round: the lake glintRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #6 round: the trunk and the Y branchesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the thin stemsLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • White canvas or canvas board
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

STEP 1 OF 11

Paint the sunset sky

  1. Paint the top fifth of the canvas Dusk blue with long side-to-side strokes.
  2. Below it, switch to Sunset orange and keep the long strokes going all the way to the bottom edge. X-stroke where the blue and orange meet so they blend while wet.
  3. Brush Sun yellow into the orange in a soft glow a little left of center, about 40 percent of the way down.
  4. Dab a round Sun yellow sun in the middle of that glow.
Paints for this step3 paints, 3 new
  • Dusk blue new3 parts white, 1 part ultramarine blue, a tiny touch of red
  • Sunset orange new2 parts yellow, 1 part red, a touch of white
  • Sun yellow new3 parts white, 1 part yellow

Brushes

2 inch flat#8 round

Strokes

Long side-to-side strokes. Pull the 2 inch flat all the way across the canvas in one go, edge to edge, so the sky has no stops or patches.

X stroke. Where blue meets orange, criss-cross the flat in small overlapping X shapes until the band between them is soft.

Watch out: Stopping at the horizon. Paint the orange all the way down; the hills and lavender go on top of it.

Watch out: Letting blue and orange mix into grey. Wipe the brush between colors and blend only where they meet.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How this picture was made Render · 2 tries · $0.039

Why this step, now: Everything else sits on the sky, and running it to the bottom edge means no white canvas ever peeks through the hills or lavender.

Why this tool: The sky runs under everything later (hills, tree, lavender), so no filter or masking of the finish can show it; rendered from the finish, then redone once because the first render put the sun right of center.

No diagram: A gradient and a round sun; the words say where each color goes.

STEP 2 OF 11

Add the sunset clouds

  1. Dab big Coral cloud masses across the top right with the corner of the 1 inch flat, sweeping down toward the center.
  2. Add a second group of clouds on the upper left, and a few thin cloud bands across the middle, smaller as they get near the sun.
  3. Leave patches of blue showing between the clouds at the top.
  4. Dry brush Sun yellow along the cloud edges that face the sun.
Paints for this step3 paints, 1 new
  • Coral cloud new2 parts red, 1 part yellow, 1 part white
  • Sun yellow from step 1, mix more if it has dried3 parts white, 1 part yellow
  • Sunset orange from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts yellow, 1 part red, a touch of white

Add a little more red to Coral cloud for the darker cloud bottoms.

Brushes

1 inch flatold stiff flat

Strokes

Dabbing with the brush corner. Tap the corner of the flat in little lumpy clusters so each cloud has a bumpy, puffy edge.

Dry brushing. Wipe most of the Sun yellow off the stiff flat, then skim it lightly along the cloud edges so it catches only the top of the paint.

Watch out: Making every cloud the same size. Keep the big ones at the top right and let them shrink toward the horizon.

Watch out: Covering all the blue. The blue gaps make the clouds glow.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How this picture was made Render · 1 try · $0.019

Why this step, now: Clouds go straight on the wet-looking sky and are the next farthest thing; doing them before the mountains lets their bottoms tuck behind the ridges.

Why this tool: The clouds sit over the sky and under the balloon and tree; no filter can remove the later layers and invent the sky behind them.

No diagram: Clouds are a texture made by repeating one dabbing mark, and the words say where the big and small ones go.

STEP 3 OF 11

Paint the far mountains

  1. Paint the far mountain ridges in Mountain violet: a big peak on the left, a second one right of the sun, and lower ridges at the far right. Press the edge of the 1 inch flat for the ridge line, then fill down.
  2. Add a little more blue to the mix and paint a lower row of darker hills across the whole width with horizontal strokes.
  3. Pull one thin line of Sun yellow under the sun for the lake glint, running a little to the right.
Paints for this step2 paints, 1 new
  • Mountain violet new2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part red, 2 parts white
  • Sun yellow from step 1, mix more if it has dried3 parts white, 1 part yellow

Mountain violet plus a little extra ultramarine for the lower hills.

Brushes

1 inch flat#4 round

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the flat's long edge on the canvas along the ridge, lift, and move along; it makes a crisp mountain line in one touch.

Horizontal strokes. Fill the lower hills with flat side-to-side strokes so they sit down and stay quiet.

Watch out: Sharp, dark mountains. Keep them soft and pale; far things look lighter and bluer.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 11

Paint the valley and the village

  1. Paint the fields on the left in horizontal strokes of Golden ochre with a little Leaf green.
  2. Build the village about a fifth of the way in from the left: small cream boxes (Sun yellow with a touch of Terracotta) for the walls, then Terracotta roofs on top, and a small tower on the biggest house.
  3. Press and lift the #4 round in Deep green to pull a few tall, thin cypresses up among the houses and one to the right of center.
  4. Tap Deep green bushes and tree lines across the middle with the stiff flat. Leave the lower right orange; the golden hill goes there next.
Paints for this step5 paints, 4 new
  • Golden ochre new3 parts yellow, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of red
  • Leaf green new2 parts yellow, 1 part ultramarine blue, a touch of white
  • Deep green new2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna
  • Terracotta new2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red, 1 part white
  • Sun yellow from step 1, mix more if it has dried3 parts white, 1 part yellow

Cream walls: Sun yellow with a touch of Terracotta.

Brushes

1 inch flat#4 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Building from simple pieces. Each house is just a box, then a low triangle roof on top. Paint all the boxes first, then all the roofs.

Press and lift. For a cypress, set the round down at the base, press so it spreads, then pull up and lift so it tapers to a point.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff flat straight onto the canvas for the round bushes; don't drag it.

Watch out: Detailing the village. It's far away: a few boxes and roofs are enough.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 11

Paint the golden hillside

  1. Paint the big hillside with Golden ochre, starting near the center and sweeping up to the right edge, about halfway down the canvas at its top. Follow the slope with your strokes.
  2. While it's wet, blend a little Sunset orange into the top of the hill where the sun hits it.
  3. Tap a row of Deep green bushes along the hill's lower edge with the stiff flat, then a few Leaf green dabs on their tops.
  4. The bottom third stays orange for now; the lavender covers it next.

  • Golden ochre from step 4, mix more if it has dried3 parts yellow, 1 part burnt sienna, a touch of red
  • Sunset orange from step 1, mix more if it has dried2 parts yellow, 1 part red, a touch of white
  • Deep green from step 4, mix more if it has dried2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna
  • Leaf green from step 4, mix more if it has dried2 parts yellow, 1 part ultramarine blue, a touch of white

Brushes

1 inch flatold stiff flat

Strokes

Strokes that follow the slope. Pull the flat on a diagonal, up to the right, the way the hill rises; a few streaks show the grass direction.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff flat for each bush, dark first, then a lighter dab on top where the light falls.

Watch out: Painting the hill in flat side-to-side strokes. Follow the slope so it reads as a hill.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 11

Paint the oak tree

  1. Pull the trunk up from the top of the hill near the right edge with the #6 round in Bark brown, splitting it into a Y just under where the crown will go.
  2. Dab a wide crown in Deep green with the stiff flat, about one and a half times as wide as it is tall, centered over the trunk.
  3. Push its edge out into bumpy clusters so it isn't a smooth ball.
  4. Dab Leaf green on the upper left of the clusters, where the sun hits.
Paints for this step3 paints, 1 new
  • Deep green from step 4, mix more if it has dried2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna
  • Leaf green from step 4, mix more if it has dried2 parts yellow, 1 part ultramarine blue, a touch of white
  • Bark brown new2 parts burnt sienna, a touch of ultramarine blue

Brushes

#6 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the round hard at the base of the trunk, then lift as you pull up so it narrows; split into two arms at the top.

Dabbing. Tap the stiff flat in little bunches for the leaf clusters; turn the brush between taps so they don't line up.

Watch out: Making the crown a smooth ball. Keep the edge bumpy.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 11

Paint the lavender rows

  1. Find the spot the rows point to: right of center (about 60 percent across), where the lavender meets the bottom of the hill.
  2. With the #8 round, paint two Path brown dirt paths starting at that spot and fanning down: one to just left of center at the bottom edge, one to about three quarters across. Make them wider toward the bottom.
  3. Fill the row between the paths and the rows on each side with Lavender purple, curving your strokes the way each row runs.
  4. Blend Deep lavender into the base of each row while it's wet.
Paints for this step3 paints, 3 new
  • Lavender purple new2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part red, 1 part white
  • Deep lavender new2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part red, a touch of burnt sienna
  • Path brown new2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part red, 1 part white

Brushes

#8 round1 inch flat

Strokes

Strokes that follow the rows. Pull the flat from the far end of each row toward you, the way the row runs, so the stroke lines point back to the spot.

Wet blending. Lay Deep lavender along the bottom of a row and brush it up into the wet purple a little, so it fades.

Watch out: Rows that don't meet. Every path and row should point back to the same spot.

Watch out: Adding flowers now. These are smooth purple shapes; the spikes come next.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 11

Add the lavender flowers

  1. Tap Lavender purple with the stiff flat along the far rows in tiny dabs, just enough to make them look bumpy.
  2. In the front rows, flick thin Deep green stems up from the bottom of each row with the liner.
  3. On each front stem, dab a short column of small Light lavender strokes with the #4 round. Make the spikes biggest at the bottom of the canvas and smaller toward the back.

  • Light lavender newLavender purple plus 2 parts white
  • Lavender purple from step 7, mix more if it has dried2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part red, 1 part white
  • Deep green from step 4, mix more if it has dried2 parts ultramarine blue, 1 part yellow, 1 part burnt sienna

Brushes

old stiff flatLiner (#1 or #0)#4 round

Strokes

Dabbing. Tap the stiff flat lightly so only the tips of the bristles touch; it leaves many tiny marks at once.

Flicking. Start at the base of a row and flick the liner up and slightly outward, lifting as you go, for a thin stem.

Press and lift. For each flower bud, press the round's tip down so it spreads into a little oval, then lift; stack three or four up the stem.

Watch out: Big spikes in the back rows. Keep them tiny far away so the field has depth.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 9 OF 11

Paint the hot air balloon

  1. Lightly outline the balloon in the upper left: a big circle near the top (its left edge about a fifth of the way across), tapering into a short narrow neck below.
  2. Paint the middle stripe Balloon teal straight down the center, then work outward: red, yellow, teal, red, each stripe curving to follow the outline and getting narrower toward the edges.
  3. Paint a dark Bark brown band across the bottom of the neck.
  4. Paint the basket as a small Bark brown rectangle a short way below the neck.

Brushes

#8 round#4 round

Strokes

Building from simple pieces. Start with the circle, then the taper below it; only then split it into stripes like the sections of an orange.

Curved strokes. Pull each stripe from top to bottom in one curved stroke that bows outward like the side of the balloon.

Watch out: Straight stripes. Curve each one with the outline, or the balloon looks flat.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 10 OF 11

Shade the balloon and add the ropes

  1. Dry brush a little Deep lavender down the right side of the balloon, over every stripe it crosses, so the right edge is darker.
  2. Darken the lower part of the envelope near the neck with a thin glaze of Bark brown.
  3. Pull thin ropes from the neck down to the basket with the liner.

Brushes

#4 roundLiner (#1 or #0)

Strokes

Dry brushing. Wipe most of the paint off and drag the round down the stripe's right side, so the dark catches on the texture and fades out.

Liner lines. Thin the paint with a drop of water, rest your little finger on the canvas, and pull each rope in one steady stroke.

Watch out: Too much shading. A soft dark edge is enough; the highlights in the last step bring the color back.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Why this tool: The shading sits between the flat balloon and the finished one; no filter can add shading or take highlights away.

Why a diagram: Shading has to follow the balloon's round shape, and where the dark goes isn't obvious from a finished-looking picture.

Final highlights

Strokes

Dotting. Touch the liner's tip straight down on each spike top for a tiny bright point.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A hot air balloon over a lavender field at sunset, with hills, a village, and an oak tree

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or page around it; the whole frame is the scene.

A sunset landscape with a striped hot air balloon as the star, a lone oak on a golden hill, and lavender rows pulling the eye to the sun. The photo is already a painted illustration, so it's busy rather than messy: hundreds of lavender spikes, puffy clouds, a tiny village. The hard parts for a beginner are making the lavender rows line up in perspective and making the balloon look round; the lesson should be about painting back to front over one big glowing sky.

Subject: A striped hot air balloon drifting over a lavender field at sunset, with rolling golden hills, a small hilltop village, and a lone oak tree on the right.
Focal point: The striped balloon in the upper left, balanced by the oak tree on the right; the lavender rows lead the eye to the setting sun in the middle.
Light: The sun sits low on the horizon just left of center, so the sky glows orange and yellow there, cloud edges facing it are lit gold, and the hillside and lavender tips catch warm light.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sky gradient with the sun
  2. sunset clouds
  3. far mountains and hills, lake glint
  4. valley fields, village, cypresses, distant tree lines
  5. golden hillside and its bushes
  6. oak tree on the hill
  7. lavender rows and dirt paths

  9. hot air balloon

Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

It's a deep landscape with clear layers from far to near (sky, clouds, mountains, valley, hill, tree, lavender), which is exactly what painting along back to front on a white canvas is built for. Each layer goes straight on top of the one behind it, and the warm sky showing through gaps ties the whole picture together.

Passed onBlock in, then build up

Toning the canvas brown and sketching first would dull this glowing sunset, and the block-in step would have to flatten the whole scene at once. The paint-along order gives a beginner one part of the scene per step, which suits this many layers better.

Why the steps go in this order11 steps

Strictly back to front: the sky runs to the bottom edge first so its strokes stay long, then clouds, far mountains, the valley and village, the golden hill, and the oak on top of it. The lavender field covers the bottom as smooth rows, then gets its flower spikes. The balloon comes after the landscape as the main subject, with its flat stripes, shading, and highlights as separate steps the way a teacher would do them.

  1. 1. Paint the sunset sky

    Everything else sits on the sky, and running it to the bottom edge means no white canvas ever peeks through the hills or lavender.

  2. 2. Add the sunset clouds

    Clouds go straight on the wet-looking sky and are the next farthest thing; doing them before the mountains lets their bottoms tuck behind the ridges.

  3. 3. Paint the far mountains

    The farthest land, painted pale so the closer layers can be darker and warmer.

  4. 4. Paint the valley and the village

    The middle distance: fields, village, cypresses, and tree lines, all at about the same distance, so one step.

  5. 5. Paint the golden hillside

    The hill is in front of the valley and behind the lavender, and the oak needs it underneath.

  6. 6. Paint the oak tree

    The tree stands on the hill, so it goes on after the hill and before the nearer lavender.

  7. 7. Paint the lavender rows

    The nearest ground. Smooth rows first so the perspective is right before any texture goes on.

  8. 8. Add the lavender flowers

    Texture comes after the shape it sits on; the spikes are the lavender's texture.

  9. 9. Paint the hot air balloon

    The main subject gets its own base step: flat curved stripes over the finished sky.

  10. 10. Shade the balloon and add the ropes

    Shading is a separate step so the beginner sees the balloon turn round before the highlights.

  11. 11. Final highlights

    The brightest touches go last, on top of everything.

Where Claude drew diagrams5 steps, free

Four steps add shaped or structured things a beginner couldn't start from the picture alone (the village, the oak, the lavender rows' perspective, the balloon), and the balloon's shading follows its round shape, so five steps got diagrams. Two instructions were corrected to match the pictures: the sun and the rows' meeting point.

  • Step 4: Paint the valley and the village beginner check

    Noticed: Buildings appear whole in this step, and a beginner would try to paint windows and walls instead of the few boxes the picture really shows.

    Pieces: A village is boxes with low roofs on top, so: wall boxes first, then roofs and the tower, then cypresses pulled up last with press and lift.

  • Step 6: Paint the oak tree beginner check

    Noticed: A shaped object (a tree) appears whole, and where the trunk splits into the crown isn't clear in the picture.

    Pieces: A tree is a trunk that splits into a Y, so the trunk comes first; the crown is one wide oval, then bumpy clusters on its edge, then the light side.

  • Step 7: Paint the lavender rows beginner check

    Noticed: The rows' placement depends on perspective: every row and path has to point back to one spot, and the picture alone doesn't make that spot obvious.

    Pieces: Perspective first: one point, then the two paths fanning out from it, then the rows filled between and beside them.

  • Step 9: Paint the hot air balloon beginner check

    Noticed: The main subject appears whole, and its curved stripes depend on its round shape.

    Pieces: A balloon is a sphere with a cone under it: a circle first, then the taper to the neck, then the stripes split like orange sections, widest in the middle, then the neck band and basket.

  • Step 10: Shade the balloon and add the ropes beginner check

    Noticed: Shading has to follow the balloon's round shape, and where the dark goes isn't obvious from a finished-looking picture.

    Pieces: Starts from the balloon's pieces (already painted), adds a crescent of dark down the right side, then the ropes to the basket.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A gradient and a round sun; the words say where each color goes.
  • Step 2: Clouds are a texture made by repeating one dabbing mark, and the words say where the big and small ones go.
  • Step 3: Two soft ridge lines and a band below; the picture and words make the shape obvious.
  • Step 5: One sloping shape whose start and top are given in the words, plus dabbed bushes.
  • Step 8: A repeated mark (stem plus stacked dabs) that the words describe step by step.
  • Step 11: Small touches on parts already painted; the words say where.
What the reviewer caught3 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check The balloon's teal stripes came out bright royal blue instead of the photo's muted teal blue-green.
  • Finish check The big sunlit hillside under the tree turned yellow-green instead of the photo's warm golden ochre with orange light.
  • Round 1 Step 1: The sun sits right of center (about 53 percent across); from step 2 through the finished painting it is just left of center (about 44 percent), so the sun jumps between step 1 and step 2. (redone)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Write positions in the plan from measured coordinates in the finish, not from a glance. I wrote the sun as right of center; it rendered there and needed a paid redo.
  • Mean shift at strength 3 barely changes an already-painted illustration; go straight to strength 5 for photos that are paintings already.
  • The balloon-shading render came out darker and duller than the finish; for a step between flat color and highlights, the step text should say the highlights bring the color back.
